problem: The lead says the jet is 'turned through almost 180°', but Section 1 correctly says a bucket turns it through about 165°. A student skimming the lead will carry the wrong deflection angle into Vw2 = u + kVr1 cos δ and get a sign or magnitude error.
fix: Say in the lead: 'is turned through about 165°, not a full 180°'.

problem: The head range given (roughly 100 m to over 1000 m) starts lower and ends lower than the usual textbook range; Pelton units are normally quoted from about 150–300 m up to nearly 2000 m for the largest units.
fix: Write: 'Pelton units suit heads from about 150 m up to nearly 2000 m in the largest units, as in Himalayan run-of-river plants.'

problem: The chapter defines speed ratio as φ = u/V1 and gives 0.46. Some textbooks define speed ratio as u/√(2gH), so a student meeting the other convention in a question paper will use the wrong number.
fix: Add one sentence: 'Some books define speed ratio as u/√(2gH); that value is about 0.45 and equals φ·Cv, so do not mix the two.'

problem: The trap warns against Vw2 = u − kVr1 cos δ using δ = 165° but never says how that other form arises, so a student who has seen Vw2 = u − Vr2 cos θ in another book cannot tell which angle is meant.
fix: Add: 'Some books use the outlet vane angle θ = 180° − δ (about 15° here) and write Vw2 = u − kVr1 cos θ; the two forms give the same number, but never mix δ and θ.'

problem: The reason given (outgoing water would hit the following bucket) is the textbook reason, but it is not true at the design point: at exactly u = V1/2 a full 180° turn would leave the water with zero absolute velocity. The interference argument only holds away from u = V1/2.
fix: Answer: 'At u = V1/2 a 180° bucket would leave the water with almost no absolute velocity, but at any other bucket speed the water would leave with a backward velocity and strike the back of the following bucket. A 165° turn keeps the outlet whirl small over the whole operating range without that interference.'

problem: The note 'net head H' is attached to the penstock, but the net head is the head available at the nozzle after penstock friction, so the label can mislead a student into using the gross head.
fix: Label the penstock node as 'gross head available' and put 'net head H = gross head − penstock friction loss' on the nozzle node.
